---
title: "Heterogeneous households and monetary policy"
page-layout: article
---

Households differ in productivity and wealth. Their saving decisions determine the
asset distribution. We include this distribution in the state when solving for aggregate prices.
We first solve the economy without aggregate risk, then introduce monetary-policy shocks.

::: {.lesson-links}
[View notebook on GitHub]({{< meta repo-blob >}}/examples/hankmp/notebooks/hankmp.ipynb){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm}
:::

The script coordinates separate model, analysis, and plotting files, as in the paper's
replication package. Its saved networks are the trained networks from that package, so the
script reproduces the paper's solution without retraining. Run it from the environment
described in [Setting up Python](../setup.qmd).

## Model

### Households

Household $i$ chooses consumption $C_t^i$, labor $H_t^i$, and bonds $B_t^i$ to maximize

$$E_0\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^t\left[
\frac{(C_t^i)^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}-\chi\frac{(H_t^i)^{1+\eta}}{1+\eta}\right].$$

Its budget and borrowing constraint are

$$C_t^i+B_t^i=W_te^{s_t^i}H_t^i+
\frac{R_{t-1}}{\Pi_t}B_{t-1}^i+(Div_t-T_t)e^{s_t^i},\qquad B_t^i\geq\underline B=0.$$

Here $R_t$ is the gross nominal interest rate and $\Pi_t$ is gross inflation.
Idiosyncratic log productivity has an AR(1) transition. In each simulated panel of
households, we recenter the draws so that mean productivity is one,

$$\widetilde s_{t+1}^i=\rho_s s_t^i+\sigma_s\epsilon_{t+1}^{s,i},\qquad
s_{t+1}^i=\widetilde s_{t+1}^i-\log\left(\frac1L\sum_{j=1}^L e^{\widetilde s_{t+1}^j}\right),$$

where $L$ is the number of households in the panel.

The innovations $\epsilon^{s,i}$ and $\epsilon^{mp}$ are independent standard normals.
The optimality conditions are

$$\chi(H_t^i)^\eta=(C_t^i)^{-\sigma}W_te^{s_t^i},$$

$$1=\beta R_t E_t\left[\left(\frac{C_t^i}{C_{t+1}^i}\right)^\sigma
\frac{1}{\Pi_{t+1}}\right]+\mu_t^i,\qquad
\mu_t^i\geq0,\quad\mu_t^i(B_t^i-\underline B)=0.$$

### Firms, policy, and markets

Output equals effective labor, $Y_t=N_t=\int e^{s_t^i}H_t^i\,di$.
With unit productivity, real marginal cost equals the wage, $\Psi_t=W_t$.
Rotemberg price adjustment gives

$$\varphi\log\Pi_t=(1-\epsilon)+\epsilon \Psi_t+
\varphi E_t\left[\frac{\Pi_{t+1}}{R_t}\log\Pi_{t+1}\frac{Y_{t+1}}{Y_t}\right].$$

Profits are $Div_t=Y_t-W_tN_t-\tfrac12\varphi(\log\Pi_t)^2Y_t$.
The nominal interest rate follows

$$R_t=R_{DSS}+\theta_\Pi(\Pi_t-1)+mp_t,$$

$$mp_{t+1}=\rho_{mp}mp_t+\sigma_{mp}\epsilon_{t+1}^{mp}.$$

Taxes $T_t=(R_{t-1}/\Pi_t-1)D$ service fixed public debt $D$. Market clearing requires

$$\int B_t^i\,di=D,\qquad
\int C_t^i\,di+\tfrac12\varphi(\log\Pi_t)^2Y_t=Y_t.$$

### Calibration

The household parameters come from the SSJ steady-state solve, which targets a
steady-state nominal rate of 1.005. The code uses them at full precision.
The monetary-shock persistence $\rho_{mp}$ varies over $[0.5, 0.7]$ during training
and is evaluated at 0.6.

| Household parameters | Value | Aggregate parameters | Value |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Discount factor $\beta$ | 0.982244 | Demand elasticity $\epsilon$ | 6 |
| Risk aversion $\sigma$ | 2 | Price adjustment $\varphi$ | 60 |
| Labor curvature $\eta$ | 2 | Inflation response $\theta_\Pi$ | 1.5 |
| Labor disutility $\chi$ | 0.786433 | Public debt $D$ | 5.6 |
| Productivity persistence $\rho_s$ | 0.966 | Monetary persistence $\rho_{mp}$ | 0.6, trained over $[0.5, 0.7]$ |
| Productivity shock SD $\sigma_s$ | 0.129271 | Monetary shock SD $\sigma_{mp}$ | 0.0025 |

## Neural network solution

### Formulation

Each household's state is $(B_{t-1}^i,s_t^i)$. The aggregate state contains the joint
household distribution, the lagged nominal interest rate, and the current monetary shock.
We represent the distribution with 100 households sorted by assets. A separate panel
of $L=100$ households evaluates individual optimality conditions.
The estimated and calibrated parameter sets are

$$\tilde\Theta=\{\rho_{mp}\},\qquad
\bar\Theta=\{\beta,\sigma,\eta,\chi,\rho_s,\sigma_s,\epsilon,\varphi,\theta_\Pi,D,\sigma_{mp}\},$$

so every network takes $\rho_{mp}$ as an input.

The solution has two stages.

1. **Deterministic steady state (DSS).** Idiosyncratic risk remains active while aggregate
   risk is absent. One network predicts household labor and another predicts $(R_{DSS},Y_{DSS})$.
   Inflation is one and the wage is $(\epsilon-1)/\epsilon$.
2. **Stochastic economy.** Initialize the household network with the DSS weights. Train it
   together with an aggregate network that returns $(\Pi_t,W_t)$, and keep the DSS network fixed.

Each network normalizes each input variable, projects it to 128 values, and adds these projections,
then applies four hidden layers of 128 CELU units and a linear output layer.
There is no activation after the initial projections. Once labor is predicted,
consumption follows from labor optimality and bond choices follow from the budget constraint,

$$C_t^i=\left(\frac{W_te^{s_t^i}}{\chi(H_t^i)^\eta}\right)^{1/\sigma},\qquad
B_t^i=W_te^{s_t^i}H_t^i+\frac{R_{t-1}}{\Pi_t}B_{t-1}^i+(Div_t-T_t)e^{s_t^i}-C_t^i.$$

#### Residuals and loss

The Fischer–Burmeister function $\Psi^{FB}(a,b)=a+b-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ encodes complementarity.
Let $\bar\lambda_t^i=\beta R_tE_t[(C_t^i/C_{t+1}^i)^\sigma/\Pi_{t+1}]$.
The implementation adds a numerical upper asset bound $\overline B=125$ and uses

$$F^{1,i}_t=\begin{cases}
\Psi^{FB}(B_t^i-\underline B,1-\bar\lambda_t^i), & B_t^i<0.8\overline B,\\
\Psi^{FB}(\overline B-B_t^i,\bar\lambda_t^i-1), & B_t^i\geq0.8\overline B.
\end{cases}$$

The second branch switches to the upper-bound complementarity condition. After
training, check that this numerical bound does not affect the solution.

Five aggregate residuals follow, in the same order in both stages.
$F^2$ is output consistency $Y_t-Y_{DSS}$ in the DSS stage and the Phillips curve in the
stochastic stage. $F^3=D-\langle B_t\rangle$ and
$F^4=Y_t-\langle C_t\rangle-\tfrac12\varphi(\log\Pi_t)^2Y_t$ are bond and goods market
clearing, where angle brackets denote means over the distribution panel. $F^5$ and $F^6$
are the same two conditions next period, one for each of the $M$ shock draws.

Each aggregate residual is divided by its scale before squaring. The Phillips curve is
divided by $1-\epsilon$, output and goods clearing by output, and bond clearing by $D$. For a batch of $N_{batch}$ economies, the loss is

$$
\mathcal L=\frac1{N_{batch}}\sum_{b=1}^{N_{batch}}\left[
\alpha_1\frac1L\sum_{i=1}^L(F^{1,i,b})^2+\sum_{j=2}^{4}\alpha_j(F^{j,b})^2
+\frac1M\sum_{m=1}^M\left(\alpha_5(F^{5,b,m})^2+\alpha_6(F^{6,b,m})^2\right)\right],
$$

with every weight $\alpha_j$ equal to one.

#### Training

Each iteration takes 10 internal updates on a batch of $N_{batch}=50$ economies. Each update
draws $M=100$ next-period shocks as antithetic pairs to approximate the expectations. The
shocks that simulate the panel forward are not paired. Every 10 iterations, before the panel
advances, $\rho_{mp}$ is redrawn for each economy and the panel advances 5 periods. After the
updates, the panel advances $T^{sim}=5$ periods. In the stochastic stage, if any household's bonds
leave $[\underline B-50,\overline B+50]$, the panel restarts from the steady state.

Each stage runs 20,000 iterations with AdamW, weight decay 0.01, and gradient-norm
clipping at 1. The learning rate warms up from $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-4}$ over the first
2,000 iterations, then follows cosine annealing to $10^{-8}$. Idiosyncratic shock
standard deviations rise from 10% to 100% of their target over the first 1,000
iterations. In the stochastic stage, monetary shocks start at 10% and rise to full
size between iterations 1,000 and 2,000.

### In the code

#### Set the parameters and shocks

`ranges` lists the one parameter that varies during training. The aggregate productivity
input `z` is retained from the replication package with zero shock variance. `Rn_ss` supplies
the reference rate used to initialize the simulated panels. The DSS network learns its own rate.

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp.py"}
parameters = {
    # Households, from the SSJ steady-state solve.
    "beta": 0.9822435537836073,
    "gamma": 2.0,
    "eta": 2.0,
    "chi": 0.7864334221642553,
    "rho_s": 0.966,
    "sigma_s": 0.12927103310486848,
    "B": 5.6,
    "phipi": 1.5,
    # Borrowing limit and numerical upper asset bound.
    "b_min": -0.0,
    "b_max": 125.0,
    # Reference nominal rate for initialization. The DSS network learns R_DSS.
    "Rn_ss": 1.005,
    # Dormant TFP process.
    "rho_z": 0.0,
    "sigma_z": 0.0,
    # Monetary-policy shock.
    "rho_mps": 0.6,
    "sigma_mps": 0.0025,
    # Firms.
    "varphi": 60.0,
    "theta": 6.0,
}
ranges = {"rho_mps": torch.distributions.Uniform(0.5, 0.7)}  # Varies during training.
shocks_ind = {"s": torch.distributions.Normal(0.0, 1.0)}
shocks_agg = {
    "z": torch.distributions.Normal(0.0, 1.0),
    "mps": torch.distributions.Normal(0.0, 1.0),
}
```

The code names map to the symbols above as follows.

| Code | Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n` | $H_t^i$ | labor |
| `b`, `b_min`, `b_max` | $B_t^i$, $\underline B$, $\overline B$ | bonds and their bounds |
| `s` | $s_t^i$ | log productivity |
| `gamma` | $\sigma$ | risk aversion |
| `theta` | $\epsilon$ | demand elasticity |
| `varphi` | $\varphi$ | price-adjustment cost |
| `phipi` | $\theta_\Pi$ | Taylor-rule inflation response |
| `B` | $D$ | public debt |
| `tau` | | tax per unit of $e^{s_t^i}$ |
| `Psi` | $\Psi_t$ | real marginal cost |
| `NE` | $N_t$ | productivity-weighted labor, equal to output $Y_t$ |
| `Rn`, `Rn_lag`, `Rn_dss` | $R_t$, $R_{t-1}$, $R_{DSS}$ | gross nominal rates |
| `mps`, `rho_mps`, `sigma_mps` | $mp_t$, $\rho_{mp}$, $\sigma_{mp}$ | monetary shock |
| `lambda_comp` | $\bar\lambda_t^i$ | expected Euler term |
| `Efp` | | expected Phillips-curve term |
| `res_fb`, `res_nkpc` or `res_y` | $F^1$, $F^2$ | household residual, Phillips curve (output consistency in the DSS) |
| `res_bond`, `res_product` | $F^3$, $F^4$ | market clearing today |
| `res_bond_next`, `res_product_next` | $F^5$, $F^6$ | market clearing next period |
| `_ind`, `_dist` suffixes | | the $L$-household panel and the distribution panel |

#### Evaluate and transform policies

`hh_policy` sorts the distribution by assets, assembles the inputs, evaluates the household
network, and transforms its output into labor. Consumption and bond holdings are then derived
using the equations above. `agg_policy` follows the same sequence for the aggregate network,
with separate columns for inflation and the wage. The output bounds help keep trial policies
economically meaningful.

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp_model.py"}
def hh_policy(self, state_ind, state_dist, state_agg, par, mc=None):
    """Household labor n in (0.01, 2.0) from the full-model hh network (distribution sorted by assets)."""
    state_dist = self._permute_dist(state_dist.sort("b", dim=-2), mc)
    par = self._prepare_par_input(par, mc)
    out = self.hh_network(state_ind=state_ind, state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)
    n_low, n_high = 0.01, 2.0
    return n_low + torch.sigmoid(out[..., 0:1]) * (n_high - n_low)

def agg_policy(self, state_dist, state_agg, par, mc=None):
    """Aggregate policies from the agg network: inflation Pi in (0.9, 1.1) and wage W in (0.5, 1.5)."""
    state_dist = self._permute_dist(state_dist.sort("b", dim=-2), mc)
    par = self._prepare_par_input(par, mc)
    out = self.agg_network(state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)
    Pi = 0.9 + torch.sigmoid(out[..., 0:1]) * (1.1 - 0.9)
    W = 0.5 + torch.sigmoid(out[..., 1:2]) * (1.5 - 0.5)
    return Pi, W
```

#### Form the equilibrium errors

The method below evaluates current policies and calculates consumption and bonds. It then
advances the states with the shock draws in `e`, evaluates future policies, averages over the
draws, and forms the six residuals.
`detach_next=True` holds future-policy predictions fixed when differentiating today's
equation errors. Two switches appear in the code. `known_dss` is off in this example,
so the learned $(R_{DSS},Y_{DSS})$ are used. `adjusted_residuals` is on, which applies
the scaling described above.

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp_model.py"}
def residuals(self, e, mc, detach_next=True, scale_ind=1, scale_agg=1, adjusted_residuals=False):
    par = self.par_draw
    ss = self.ss
    state_ind, state_dist, state_agg = self.state_ind, self.state_dist, self.state_agg
    e_ind, e_dist, e_agg = e

    # Current period: policies -> aggregates -> household budgets
    if self.known_dss:
        Rn_dss, Y_dss = ss.Rn, ss.Y
    else:
        Rn_dss, Y_dss = self.dss_policy(par=par)
    n_ind = self.hh_policy(state_ind=state_ind, state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)
    n_dist = self.hh_policy(state_ind=state_dist, state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)
    Pi, W = self.agg_policy(state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)

    Rn_lag = state_agg.Rn_lag
    NE = torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist.s) * n_dist, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    Y = torch.exp(state_agg.z) * NE
    T = self._bond_tax(par.B, Rn_lag, Pi)
    tau = T / torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist.s), dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    Psi = W / torch.exp(state_agg.z)
    Rn = Rn_dss + par.phipi * (Pi - 1) + state_agg.mps   # Taylor rule (ELB stripped)

    c_ind = ((W * torch.exp(state_ind.s)) / (ss.chi * n_ind ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    c_dist = ((W * torch.exp(state_dist.s)) / (ss.chi * n_dist ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    div = Y - W * NE - 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi) ** 2 * Y
    div_ind = div * torch.exp(state_ind.s)
    div_dist = div * torch.exp(state_dist.s)
    wealth_ind = W * torch.exp(state_ind.s) * n_ind + Rn_lag / Pi * state_ind.b + div_ind - tau * torch.exp(state_ind.s)
    wealth_dist = W * torch.exp(state_dist.s) * n_dist + Rn_lag / Pi * state_dist.b + div_dist - tau * torch.exp(state_dist.s)
    b_ind = wealth_ind - c_ind
    b_dist = wealth_dist - c_dist
    C = torch.mean(c_dist, dim=-2, keepdim=True)

    # Next period
    shape_ind = e_ind.s.shape
    shape_dist = e_dist.s.shape
    shape_agg = e_agg.z.shape

    s_ind_next = self._ar1_next(state_ind.s, e_ind.s, par, scale_ind)
    s_dist_next = self._ar1_next(state_dist.s, e_dist.s, par, scale_ind)
    z = (1 - par.rho_z) * ss.z + par.rho_z * state_agg.z + e_agg.z * par.sigma_z * scale_agg
    mps = par.rho_mps * state_agg.mps + e_agg.mps * par.sigma_mps * scale_agg

    state_ind_next = State({"b": b_ind.expand(shape_ind), "s": s_ind_next})
    state_dist_next = State({"b": b_dist.expand(shape_dist), "s": s_dist_next})
    state_agg_next = State({"z": z, "mps": mps, "Rn_lag": Rn.expand(shape_agg)})

    with torch.set_grad_enabled(not detach_next):
        n_ind_next = self.hh_policy(mc=mc, state_ind=state_ind_next, state_dist=state_dist_next, state_agg=state_agg_next, par=par)
        n_dist_next = self.hh_policy(mc=mc, state_ind=state_dist_next, state_dist=state_dist_next, state_agg=state_agg_next, par=par)
        Pi_next, W_next = self.agg_policy(mc=mc, state_dist=state_dist_next, state_agg=state_agg_next, par=par)

    NE_next = torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist_next.s) * n_dist_next, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    Y_next = torch.exp(state_agg_next.z) * NE_next
    T_next = self._bond_tax(par.B, state_agg_next.Rn_lag, Pi_next)
    tau_next = T_next / torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist_next.s), dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    div_next = Y_next - W_next * NE_next - 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi_next) ** 2 * Y_next
    div_dist_next = div_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s)
    wealth_dist_next = W_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s) * n_dist_next + Rn / Pi_next * state_dist_next.b + div_dist_next - tau_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s)
    c_ind_next = ((W_next * torch.exp(state_ind_next.s)) / (ss.chi * n_ind_next ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    c_dist_next = ((W_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s)) / (ss.chi * n_dist_next ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    b_dist_next = wealth_dist_next - c_dist_next
    C_next = torch.mean(c_dist_next, dim=-2, keepdim=True)

    q = par.beta * (c_ind_next / c_ind) ** (-par.gamma)
    Efp = torch.mean((Pi_next / Rn) * torch.log(Pi_next) * (Y_next / Y), dim=0)
    lambda_comp = torch.mean(q * Rn / Pi_next, dim=0)

    # Equilibrium residuals (Euler/FB, NKPC, bond clearing, goods clearing)
    res_fb = torch.where(
        b_ind < 0.8 * par.b_max,
        fisher_burmeister(b_ind - par.b_min, 1 - lambda_comp),
        fisher_burmeister(par.b_max - b_ind, lambda_comp - 1),  # corrected sign (upper bound)
    )
    res_nkpc = par.varphi * torch.log(Pi) - ((1 - par.theta) + par.theta * Psi + par.varphi * Efp)
    res_bond = par.B - torch.mean(b_dist, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    res_bond_next = par.B - torch.mean(b_dist_next, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    res_product = Y - (C + 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi) ** 2 * Y)
    res_product_next = Y_next - (C_next + 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi_next) ** 2 * Y_next)

    if adjusted_residuals:
        return [res_fb, res_nkpc / (1 - par.theta), res_bond / par.B, res_product / Y, res_bond_next / par.B, res_product_next / Y_next]
    return [res_fb, res_nkpc, res_bond, res_product, res_bond_next, res_product_next]
```

## The DSS residuals

The DSS version has the same structure. Inflation and the wage are fixed at their
steady-state values, the rate is the learned $R_{DSS}$, and the second residual is
output consistency instead of the Phillips curve.

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp_model.py"}
def dss_residuals(self, e, mc, detach_next=True, scale_ind=1, scale_agg=0, adjusted_residuals=False):
    par = self.par_draw
    ss = self.ss
    state_ind, state_dist, state_agg = self.state_ind, self.state_dist, self.state_agg
    e_ind, e_dist, e_agg = e

    # Current period: policies -> aggregates -> household budgets
    n_ind = self.dss_hh_policy(state_ind=state_ind, state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)
    n_dist = self.dss_hh_policy(state_ind=state_dist, state_dist=state_dist, state_agg=state_agg, par=par)
    if self.known_dss:
        Rn_dss, Y_dss = ss.Rn, ss.Y
    else:
        Rn_dss, Y_dss = self.dss_policy(par=par)

    Rn_lag = Rn_dss          # gross nominal rate on bonds (DSS: notional = SS level)
    Rn = Rn_dss              # realized gross nominal rate (DSS: no inflation gap, no mps)
    Pi = ss.Pi
    W = ss.W
    NE = torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist.s) * n_dist, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    Y = torch.exp(ss.z) * NE
    T = self._bond_tax(par.B, Rn_lag, Pi)
    tau = T / torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist.s), dim=-2, keepdim=True)

    c_ind = ((W * torch.exp(state_ind.s)) / (ss.chi * n_ind ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    c_dist = ((W * torch.exp(state_dist.s)) / (ss.chi * n_dist ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    div = Y - W * NE - 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi) ** 2 * Y
    div_ind = div * torch.exp(state_ind.s)
    div_dist = div * torch.exp(state_dist.s)
    wealth_ind = W * torch.exp(state_ind.s) * n_ind + Rn_lag / Pi * state_ind.b + div_ind - tau * torch.exp(state_ind.s)
    wealth_dist = W * torch.exp(state_dist.s) * n_dist + Rn_lag / Pi * state_dist.b + div_dist - tau * torch.exp(state_dist.s)
    b_ind = wealth_ind - c_ind
    b_dist = wealth_dist - c_dist
    C = torch.mean(c_dist, dim=-2, keepdim=True)

    # Next period
    shape_ind = e_ind.s.shape
    shape_dist = e_dist.s.shape
    shape_agg = e_agg.z.shape

    s_ind_next = self._ar1_next(state_ind.s, e_ind.s, par, scale_ind)
    s_dist_next = self._ar1_next(state_dist.s, e_dist.s, par, scale_ind)
    z = (1 - par.rho_z) * ss.z + par.rho_z * state_agg.z + e_agg.z * par.sigma_z * scale_agg
    mps = par.rho_mps * state_agg.mps + e_agg.mps * par.sigma_mps * scale_agg

    state_ind_next = State({"b": b_ind.expand(shape_ind), "s": s_ind_next})
    state_dist_next = State({"b": b_dist.expand(shape_dist), "s": s_dist_next})
    state_agg_next = State({"z": z, "mps": mps, "Rn_lag": Rn.expand(shape_agg)})

    with torch.set_grad_enabled(not detach_next):
        n_ind_next = self.dss_hh_policy(mc=mc, state_ind=state_ind_next, state_dist=state_dist_next, state_agg=state_agg_next, par=par)
        n_dist_next = self.dss_hh_policy(mc=mc, state_ind=state_dist_next, state_dist=state_dist_next, state_agg=state_agg_next, par=par)

    NE_next = torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist_next.s) * n_dist_next, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    Pi_next = ss.Pi
    W_next = ss.W
    Y_next = torch.exp(ss.z) * NE_next
    T_next = self._bond_tax(par.B, state_agg_next.Rn_lag, Pi_next)
    tau_next = T_next / torch.mean(torch.exp(state_dist_next.s), dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    div_next = Y_next - W_next * NE_next - 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi_next) ** 2 * Y_next
    div_dist_next = div_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s)
    wealth_dist_next = W_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s) * n_dist_next + Rn / Pi_next * state_dist_next.b + div_dist_next - tau_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s)
    c_ind_next = ((W_next * torch.exp(state_ind_next.s)) / (ss.chi * n_ind_next ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    c_dist_next = ((W_next * torch.exp(state_dist_next.s)) / (ss.chi * n_dist_next ** par.eta)) ** (1 / par.gamma)
    b_dist_next = wealth_dist_next - c_dist_next
    C_next = torch.mean(c_dist_next, dim=-2, keepdim=True)

    q = par.beta * (c_ind_next / c_ind) ** (-par.gamma)
    lambda_comp = torch.mean(q * Rn / Pi_next, dim=0)

    # Equilibrium residuals (Euler/FB, output, bond clearing, goods clearing)
    res_fb = torch.where(
        b_ind < 0.8 * par.b_max,
        fisher_burmeister(b_ind - par.b_min, 1 - lambda_comp),
        fisher_burmeister(par.b_max - b_ind, lambda_comp - 1),  # corrected sign (upper bound)
    )
    res_y = Y - Y_dss
    res_bond = par.B - torch.mean(b_dist, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    res_bond_next = par.B - torch.mean(b_dist_next, dim=-2, keepdim=True)
    res_product = Y - (C + 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi) ** 2 * Y)
    res_product_next = Y_next - (C_next + 0.5 * par.varphi * torch.log(Pi_next) ** 2 * Y_next)

    if adjusted_residuals:
        return [res_fb, res_y / Y, res_bond / par.B, res_product / Y, res_bond_next / par.B, res_product_next / Y_next]
    return [res_fb, res_y, res_bond, res_product, res_bond_next, res_product_next]
```
::: {.code-source}
[View in `hankmp_model.py` on GitHub]({{< meta repo-blob >}}/examples/hankmp/hankmp_model.py)
:::
:::

`loss` adds the weighted mean squared residuals into the training loss. It also returns each
unweighted equation loss for the loss plots.

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp_model.py"}
def loss(self, residuals, criterion, names, weights=None):
    """Weighted sum of per-residual MSEs (the scalar to backprop) plus the unweighted per-residual components for logging."""
    if weights is None:
        weights = [1.0] * len(residuals)
    loss = [weights[i] * criterion(r, target=torch.zeros_like(r)) for i, r in enumerate(residuals)]
    with torch.no_grad():
        loss_components = {name: torch.mean(r ** 2) for name, r in zip(names, residuals)}
    return sum(loss), loss_components
```
::: {.code-source}
[View in `hankmp_model.py` on GitHub]({{< meta repo-blob >}}/examples/hankmp/hankmp_model.py)
:::

#### Train in two stages

The repository ships the trained networks from the replication package. Leave `load_dss` and
`load_full` set to `True` to load them. Set `load_full = False` to retrain the
stochastic model, and also set `load_dss = False` to solve the DSS again. The
full-model checkpoint includes the DSS networks. Between the two stages, `warm_start_full`
copies the DSS household weights into the stochastic model's household network.

The computations are performed on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU with 32 GB of memory. The
computational time is around 43 minutes for the DSS and 46 minutes for the full equilibrium.
The GPU memory usage is 0.6 GB. Training takes far longer on a CPU.

Both stages use the same training settings.

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp.py"}
# Both stages use the same settings. Aggregate residuals are divided by their scale.
config = TrainingConfig(
    iteration=20000,
    internal=10,
    steps=5,
    batch=50,
    mc=100,
    lr=1e-4,
    eta_min=1e-8,
    adjusted_residuals=True,
    device=DEVICE,
    seed=1234,
)
```

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp.py"}
dss_path = networks / "dss.pt"
full_path = networks / "full.pt"
train_full = not load_full or not full_path.exists()
train_dss = train_full and (not load_dss or not dss_path.exists())

if train_dss:
    print("Training the deterministic steady state...")
    model.train_dss_model(config)
    model.save(networks, name="dss")
    # A new DSS needs a new full model, so delete the saved one.
    full_path.unlink(missing_ok=True)
elif train_full:
    print("Loading the deterministic steady state.")
    model.load(dss_path)
```

```{.python filename="examples/hankmp/hankmp.py"}
if train_full:
    print("Training the model with aggregate risk...")
    model.warm_start_full()
    model.train_model(config)
    model.save(networks, name="full")
else:
    print("Loading the model with aggregate risk.")
    model.load(full_path)
```

[View in `hankmp.py` on GitHub]({{< meta repo-blob >}}/examples/hankmp/hankmp.py)
:::

## Results

The analysis uses the methods of the replication package with smaller samples, so it runs
on a CPU in about 10 minutes. It compares with the SSJ reference shipped in
`examples/hankmp/outputs/reference`. The results are saved and reused. Set
`load_analysis = False` to recompute them.

### Deterministic steady state

The top panel of the figure below displays the evolution of the average loss over the
training. In the lower panels, we plot the in-training evolution of each equilibrium
condition. To facilitate convergence during training, we gradually introduce idiosyncratic
shocks by increasing their variance from a small value to their target levels over the
course of the first 1,000 iterations. The red shaded area marks this stage. The training is
successful, with clear convergence of the average loss. The breakdown of the loss into the
individual residual errors confirms that the neural network learns all policy functions of
interest effectively.

![**Convergence of the NN solution for the deterministic steady state.** The figure shows the dynamics of the mean squared error during the training of the DSS, smoothed by a moving median over 100 iterations. The upper plot shows the average loss, while the subcomponents are shown below. The shaded area indicates the period in which we scale up idiosyncratic risk. The vertical axis has a logarithmic scale.](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/dss_loss.png)

The next figure shows the bar graph of the asset distribution conditional on various levels of
productivity (10th percentile, 50th percentile, and 90th percentile) along with the policy
functions of labor supply and consumption. To be concise, we skip the values of the
deterministic steady state here. The script calculates them.

![**Policy functions.** Policy functions (labor supply in the upper panels and consumption in the lower panels) and asset distribution conditional on individual productivity (10th percentile, 50th percentile, 90th percentile).](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/dss_hh_policy_histogram.png)

### Full equilibrium

The top panel of the figure below displays the evolution of the average loss over the
training for 20,000 iterations. In the other panels, we plot the in-training evolution of
the Euler equation, the New Keynesian Phillips curve (NKPC), bond market clearing in the
current as well as next period, and goods market clearing in the current as well as next
period. As in the DSS, we gradually introduce idiosyncratic shocks over the first 1,000
iterations, marked by the red shaded area. Afterward, we introduce aggregate risk between
iterations 1,000 and 2,000. The training is successful, with clear convergence of the
average loss.

![**Convergence of the NN solution for the full equilibrium.** The figure shows the dynamics of the mean squared error during the training of the full equilibrium, smoothed by a moving median over 100 iterations. The upper plot shows the average loss, while the subcomponents are shown below. The shaded areas indicate the periods in which we scale up idiosyncratic and then aggregate risk. The vertical axis has a logarithmic scale.](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/full_loss.png)

The next step is to calculate the approximation errors *after* the training of the neural
networks has been completed. We use the same set of equilibrium conditions used during
training, which are the Euler equation, the NKPC, bond market clearing, and goods market
clearing. The absolute errors for these equations can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}
err_1 &= \left|\Psi^{FB}\left(1-\beta R_t\mathbb E_t\left[\left(\frac{C_t^i}{C_{t+1}^i}\right)^\sigma\frac{1}{\Pi_{t+1}}\right],B_t^i-\underline B\right)\right|,\\
err_2 &= \left|\frac{\varphi\log\Pi_t}{1-\epsilon}-\left(1+\frac{\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}\Psi_t+\frac{\varphi}{1-\epsilon}\mathbb E_t\left[\frac{\Pi_{t+1}}{R_t}\log\Pi_{t+1}\frac{Y_{t+1}}{Y_t}\right]\right)\right|,\\
err_3 &= \left|1-\frac{\frac1L\sum_{i=1}^L B_t^i}{D}\right|,\\
err_4 &= \left|1-\frac{\frac1L\sum_{i=1}^L C_t^i+\tfrac12\varphi(\log\Pi_t)^2Y_t}{Y_t}\right|,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $err_1$ is for the Euler equation, $err_2$ for the NKPC, $err_3$ for bond market
clearing, and $err_4$ for goods market clearing. These are the scaled residuals used in
training. We do not include bond and goods market clearing next period, as they are already
covered by their current-period counterparts. We simulate 10 economies and calculate the
approximation errors at 100 successive periods, drawing 1,000 shocks to evaluate
expectations. The replication package uses 1,000 periods, for 10,000 observations in
total. The residual errors are well
contained. The symmetry and concentration of the distributions around small values further
reinforce the reliability of the neural network solution, indicating that the approximation
performs consistently well across a wide range of simulated states.

![**Distribution of post-training approximation errors.** The figure shows the absolute error for the modified Euler equation (to account for the occasionally binding borrowing limit), the New Keynesian Phillips curve, bond market clearing, and goods market clearing. Errors are evaluated after the training of the neural networks is complete, at 100 simulated periods of 10 economies. We evaluate the expectations in the modified Euler equation and the NKPC with 1,000 Monte Carlo draws. The horizontal axis displays the $\log_{10}$ of the value, and dashed lines mark the mean $\log_{10}$ values.](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/full_euler_errors.png)

### Comparison with the sequence-space Jacobian

We now compare our neural network-based solution method to a conventional (linear)
approach, specifically the sequence-space Jacobian (SSJ) approach of Auclert et al. (2021).
For this comparison, we use the conventional linearized SSJ solution. The impulse responses
also show the nonlinear SSJ solution.

The figure below compares the asset distribution generated by our method and by the SSJ
approach. For our method, we report the distribution averaged over economies simulated with
aggregate shocks, which accounts for the presence of aggregate risk. In contrast, the
linearized SSJ solution we use assumes away aggregate uncertainty in the steady state, so its
distribution corresponds to the deterministic steady state. Despite this key difference, the
two distributions are remarkably similar. Although minor deviations are visible in the tails,
the overall shape and key moments align closely, suggesting that our method provides a highly
accurate approximation. In the paper, we report the comparison using the deterministic steady
state for both models. In this case, the resulting distributions are also remarkably similar,
as expected.

Notably, these deviations cannot be attributed solely to inaccuracies in either our method or
the SSJ approach. Instead, they stem from a fundamental difference in the economic
environments captured by the two methods. Incorporating aggregate uncertainty, as our method
does, leads poorer households to work more in response to increased precautionary motives,
resulting in fewer households clustered at the bottom of the asset distribution, as
reflected in the shorter blue bars in the lower asset bins. At the same time, this increased
labor supply and precautionary saving among the poor depresses the equilibrium real interest
rate, thereby reducing the incentive for wealthier households to save. As a result, rich
households accumulate less wealth in equilibrium, leading to a thinner right tail in the
asset distribution. This pattern is clearly illustrated by the crossing of the blue solid and
black dashed lines in the right panel, which plots the cumulative asset distribution.

Even in this relatively stylized model, the differences between the asset distributions
implied by the nonlinear (our method) and linearized (SSJ) solutions are already notable,
despite being quite small. As we will show, these differences become even more pronounced if
we increase aggregate risk.

![**Asset distribution for our neural network (NN) method for comparison with the sequence-space Jacobian method.** For the NN method, we average the distribution over 500 economies simulated with aggregate shocks. Holdings slightly below the borrowing limit are counted in the first bin. For the SSJ, we use the deterministic steady state. Left panel: The histogram of asset holdings in equilibrium. Right panel: Cumulative distribution function for the asset holdings in equilibrium.](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/full_asset_distribution.png)

The next step is to compare the two sets of policy functions that determine agents' labor
supply and consumption decisions, as shown in the figure below. The solid lines depict the
policy functions approximated using our method, while the dashed lines correspond to the
approximation obtained using the SSJ method. Each color represents one of the seven
idiosyncratic labor productivity levels considered in Auclert et al. (2021). The brown lines
correspond to the most productive agents (top productivity bin), while the blue lines
represent the least productive ones (bottom productivity bin).

These seven productivity levels are used solely for the purpose of comparing the results
from our solution method with those from SSJ. Our solution method does not rely on
discretizing the productivity space. Instead, we treat idiosyncratic labor productivity as
the outcome of a continuous AR(1) process, as specified in the model. For the purpose of this
comparison, we evaluate the policy functions at the values of the discretization in the code
made available by Auclert and coauthors.

The upshot of the comparison is twofold. First, our method successfully replicates the
policy functions approximated by the SSJ approach. Second, the main discrepancy arises in the
behavior of the most productive agents with zero assets and of low productive agents with a
large amount of assets. Both groups represent a tiny fraction of agents. Because so few
agents follow such a path, the neural network has limited data to learn from, which results
in a less accurate approximation of their behavior. Nonetheless, the inaccuracies in these
cases are fairly limited, highlighting the strong extrapolative properties of neural networks.

![**Individual policy functions comparison for the one-asset HANK model.** The figure illustrates how the policy functions for labor and consumption vary for different asset levels and different productivity levels. We compare the neural network method with the SSJ method. We use the 7 productivity levels that the discretization approach of the SSJ provides for comparison. We evaluate the policy functions at the distribution simulated with aggregate shocks (NN) and at the deterministic steady state (SSJ).](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/full_hh_policy.png)

Indeed, the effects of a monetary policy shock on the equilibrium dynamics of aggregate
variables predicted by the two methods are quite similar, as the figure below shows.

![**Impulse response functions comparison of the neural network solution and the sequence-space Jacobian approach.** The deviations from the stochastic steady state (for the NN method) and from the deterministic steady state (for the SSJ method) are reported for a one-standard-deviation negative monetary policy shock, averaged over 100 economies. L=100 and MC=100.](/assets/results/hankmp/baseline/irf.png)

## Robustness

We now test how changing the number of agents and the number of draws for the Monte Carlo
integration affects our results, and how the solution behaves for small and large shocks.
These runs come from the replication package. Their networks are not shipped with this
example, but their saved results in `examples/hankmp/outputs/robustness` are enough to draw
the figures, and section 8 of the script redraws them. They use the full analysis sizes of
the replication package, for example 2,000 economies for the asset distribution.

### Number of agents

The figure below shows the distribution of asset holdings across different levels of
discretization, with the left panel showing the histogram and the right panel the
corresponding cumulative distribution function. We compare the results for $L$=100, 200, 500,
and 1,000 agents. Each distribution is obtained by averaging across 2,000 simulated economies
(batches). The two panels illustrate that the benefit of increasing the number of tracked
agents to capture heterogeneity is minimal, since the asset distribution changes only
slightly.

![**Asset distribution for variations in the number of agents $L$.** The figure shows the histogram of asset holdings (left) and the corresponding cumulative distribution function (right) for different values of $L$ used to solve the model with our NN methods. Specifically, we consider scenarios with 100, 200, 500, and 1,000 agents in equilibrium. The distribution is averaged over 2,000 economies simulated with aggregate shocks.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/asset_distribution_agents.png)

Even more striking is the comparison based on the policy functions for labor and
consumption. The next figure shows the bar graph of the asset distribution conditional on
various levels of productivity (10th percentile, 50th percentile, and 90th percentile) along
with the policy functions of labor and consumption for 100 agents (solid line) and 1,000
(dashed line). The other individual policy function determines the agent's asset demand,
which is implied by the two individual policy functions and hence is not shown. The policy
functions exhibit minimal change as the number of tracked agents increases from 100 to 1,000,
supporting our claim that tracking more than 100 agents yields little additional benefit in
approximating the asset distribution in this one-asset HANK model.

![**Policy functions for variations in the number of agents $L$.** Policy functions (labor supply in the upper panels and consumption in the lower panels) and asset distribution conditional on individual productivity (10th percentile, 50th percentile, 90th percentile) for $L=100$ and $L=1,000$.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/hh_policy_agents.png)

Nevertheless, computing time increases rapidly as the number of agents tracked $L$ grows, as
the table below shows. The runtime ranges from 1h31min for $L=100$ to 6h12min for $L=1,000$
on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU with 32 GB of memory. Notably, even the version of the model with
1,000 agents required only 5.3 GB of memory (compared to just 0.6 GB for $L=100$). This
reflects the memory-efficient design of our solution code, which makes it feasible to run the
nonlinear one-asset HANK model on a desktop machine. For instance, solving the model with
$L=100$ took 30h38min on a recent MacBook with an Apple M4 Pro chip (14-core CPU and 20-core
GPU), using the Metal framework for macOS devices. When run on the CPU, the same task took
approximately twice as long.

| Number of agents | GPU computational time | GPU memory usage (GB) |
|---|---|---|
| $L=100$ | 1h31min | 0.6 |
| $L=200$ | 2h05min | 1.1 |
| $L=500$ | 3h35min | 2.7 |
| $L=1,000$ | 6h12min | 5.3 |

: Run time and memory usage for alternative numbers of agents, computed with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 with 32 GB of memory. Memory usage is the peak GPU memory allocated by the solver.

### Number of Monte Carlo draws

We adopt a Monte Carlo approach to approximate expectations. In general, the accuracy of this
approximation depends on using a sufficiently large number of Monte Carlo draws for
next-period shock realizations. Here, we show that this number does not need to be large
when using our neural network approach. In fact, a relatively modest number of draws is
sufficient to achieve accurate approximations. The underlying reasons are similar to those
that explain why only a limited number of agents need to be tracked in our framework.

![**Asset distribution for variations in the number of Monte Carlo draws $MC$.** The figure shows the histogram of asset holdings (left) and the related cumulative distribution function (right) for an alternative number of Monte Carlo draws for the approximation of expectations. Specifically, we consider scenarios with 100, 250, and 500 Monte Carlo draws. We average the distribution over 2,000 economies simulated with aggregate shocks.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/asset_distribution_mc.png)

![**Policy functions for variations in the number of Monte Carlo draws $MC$.** Policy functions (labor supply in the upper panels and consumption in the lower panels) and asset distribution conditional on individual productivity (10th percentile, 50th percentile, 90th percentile) for $MC=100$ and $MC=500$.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/hh_policy_mc.png)

In the baseline case with 100 agents, we vary the number of Monte Carlo draws used to
approximate next-period variables, testing with 100, 250, and 500 draws. The number of agents
is fixed at $L=100$ across these exercises. The results show that 100 Monte Carlo draws
approximate the expectations very well here. One reason that they perform so well is that we
take a new set of Monte Carlo draws during the training process for each iteration and batch,
resulting in a very good approximation over the training process.

### Size of shock volatility

The accuracy of the neural-network approximation can deteriorate when the volatility of
aggregate shocks becomes extremely small. In this case, the variation induced by the
aggregate shock may become difficult to distinguish from the numerical noise inherent in the
training procedure.

The figure below illustrates the case of very low volatility of the monetary policy shock. It
shows how the accuracy of the neural-network solution changes as we progressively reduce the
standard deviation $\sigma_{mp}$ of the monetary policy innovation. In the benchmark
specification, the standard deviation of this shock is 25 basis points. We then lower it to
the values reported in the legend at the bottom of the figure. The neural-network solution
remains stable when the standard deviation is reduced to 12.5 or 6.25 basis points. However,
at implausibly low volatility levels, 1 basis point or less, the neural network begins to
fail to capture the impulse responses to monetary policy shocks accurately.

The relevant issue is not the magnitude of the impulse responses themselves, which are
rescaled to correspond to the same shock size, but the signal-to-noise ratio encountered
during training. Our neural-network method relies on simulated data generated using a finite
number of agents, Monte Carlo integration, and a finite sample of aggregate states. These
ingredients inevitably introduce numerical noise into the training procedure. When aggregate
volatility becomes sufficiently small, the variation generated by the aggregate shock becomes
comparable to, or smaller than, this numerical noise. The neural network can then no longer
reliably distinguish the aggregate signal from noise in the simulated environment.

![**Monetary policy responses under low aggregate uncertainty in the one-asset HANK model.** The figure compares the linearized SSJ impulse responses with those generated by neural networks trained under progressively lower volatilities of the monetary policy shock. To facilitate comparison, all neural-network responses are rescaled to correspond to the same shock size.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/irf_variants_deviation.png)

### The role of large aggregate uncertainty

The next step is to illustrate how, even in a HANK model with only one aggregate shock, an
increase in aggregate risk leads to a substantial divergence between the solutions
approximated with our code and the SSJ method. At higher levels of aggregate risk,
precautionary saving behavior becomes more prominent, especially when intertwined with the
model's nonlinear features. To illustrate the effect, we scale the size of the monetary
policy shock by a factor of ten, to $\sigma_{mp}=0.025$. This run uses its own training
recipe. It trains on raw residuals with weights of 10, a step learning-rate schedule, 25
updates per iteration, and a tighter normalization of the shock input.

With a larger standard deviation of monetary policy shocks, aggregate uncertainty increases and
nonlinearities become more pronounced. This has substantial effects on the asset distribution,
households' policy functions, and the aggregate transmission of shocks. As shown in the figure
below, the share of households near the borrowing limit is now significantly lower. As our
method accounts for aggregate risk, we can now see a substantial difference compared to SSJ.

![**Asset distribution in an economy with large aggregate uncertainty.** For the NN method, we average the distribution over 2,000 economies simulated with aggregate shocks. Holdings slightly below the borrowing limit are counted in the first bin. For the linearized SSJ solution, we use the deterministic steady state, which does not account for aggregate uncertainty. Left panel: The histogram of asset holdings in equilibrium. Right panel: Cumulative distribution function for the asset holdings in equilibrium.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/big_full_asset_distribution.png)

The underlying mechanism, which we already presented for the asset distribution in the baseline
economy, is now amplified by the higher aggregate volatility. The precautionary savings motive
leads households in low productivity states to work more and consume less, relative to a
scenario with little or no aggregate risk, in order to accumulate buffer stocks of savings.
Indeed, our NN solution method shows that there is now a much lower share of households near
the borrowing limit because households have a larger precautionary motive due to larger
aggregate risks. The linearized SSJ solution does not capture these effects on the equilibrium
wealth distribution.

As these households increase savings, the equilibrium interest rate falls. In response,
high-productivity households benefit less from working, reduce their labor supply, and increase
their consumption. These responses explain why the neural network solution now diverges more
substantially from the linearized SSJ solution, which does not account for uncertainty. Part of
the gap also comes from the linearization itself, which matters more for larger shocks. In the
next figure, the two policy functions of agents now diverge more markedly and for all levels of
asset holdings. This is in large part explained by the fact that abstracting from aggregate
uncertainty is now consequential.

![**Individual policy functions in an economy with large aggregate uncertainty.** The figure illustrates how the policy functions for labor and consumption vary for different asset levels and different productivity levels. We compare the neural network method with the SSJ method. We use the 7 productivity levels that the discretization approach of the SSJ provides for comparison. We evaluate the policy functions at the distribution simulated with aggregate shocks (NN) and at the deterministic steady state (SSJ).](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/big_full_hh_policy.png)

The figure below shows the impulse response functions to a monetary policy shock under high
aggregate volatility, approximated using our method (solid red line) and the SSJ method
(dashed black line). The responses differ markedly both in the short run and in the long run.
The long-run differences can be attributed to the distinct stochastic (risky) steady states,
which are captured by our method but not by the SSJ approach.

The differences suggest that when aggregate risk is substantial, as in empirical models,
existing methodologies that rely on linearizing aggregate dynamics may fail to accurately
capture the impact of uncertainty on the long-run behavior of macro variables and the
propagation of shocks. This misrepresentation introduces inaccuracies in the short-run and
long-run dynamics of macro observables, which can distort parameter estimates and the model's
predictions.

![**Impulse response functions in an economy with large aggregate uncertainty.** The figure compares the responses generated by our neural-network solution (red solid) and the linearized SSJ solution (black dashed) following a large monetary policy shock.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/irf_big_shock_levels.png)

The last figure reports the evolution of the training loss to provide further evidence that
the neural-network solution is accurate and reliable. The line reports the loss averaged
across the equilibrium conditions that we minimize. The series is calculated as a rolling
median over 100 iterations. We facilitate training by initializing the standard deviations of
both idiosyncratic and aggregate shocks below their calibrated values and then gradually
increasing them to those levels. The shaded areas indicate the phases during which
idiosyncratic and aggregate shock volatility, respectively, are gradually scaled up. After the
temporary increases associated with these phases, the average loss declines and stabilizes at
approximately $10^{-4}$.

![**Convergence of the NN solution in an economy with large aggregate uncertainty in the one-asset HANK model.** The figure shows the mean squared error during the joint training of the individual and aggregate policy functions for the one-asset HANK model with a large monetary policy shock ($\sigma_{mp}=0.025$). The line reports the loss averaged across the equilibrium conditions that we minimize. The series is calculated as a rolling median over 100 iterations. The shaded areas indicate the periods during which the idiosyncratic and aggregate shocks are gradually introduced. The vertical axis is shown on a logarithmic scale.](/assets/results/hankmp/robustness/big_full_avg_loss.png)

## Practical advice in the case of limited access to a GPU

A practical coding strategy leverages the portability of the code architecture through a
two-stage approach if there is only limited access to a GPU. During the development stage,
the model can be designed and tested on a standard laptop (for example a MacBook, even
without using a GPU) using a relatively small number of agents, which enables fast
experimentation and debugging. Once the model's structure and performance are validated, the
same code can be executed on a high-performance desktop or server equipped with a GPU. In
this implementation stage, the greater computational power allows training neural networks
with a much larger number of agents and additional features, thereby improving the precision
of the solution and estimation results. This two-stage workflow is particularly useful in
practice, as it combines the flexibility and convenience of local model development with the
computational efficiency of large-scale implementation, greatly streamlining the research
process.
